svg.aria-label: Azure virtual network peering: both directions billed, non-transitivity as a cost multiplier, the four settings and their defaults, what global peering restricts, and the operational facts
svg.title: Azure virtual network peering: free to create, charged on both ingress and egress, and non-transitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic crosses two peerings
svg.text: Free to create, charged both ways — and non-transitive, so the hub is a hop, not a shortcut
WHAT IT COSTS
No charge for creating a peering connection. Data transfer across it is charged — and the charge
applies to ingress as well as egress, unlike most cloud networking.
Spoke-to-spoke is TWO crossings, because peering is not transitive:
Spoke A
Hub
Spoke B
2 peerings × 2 directions
The docs carry a correction: a previous version said gateway-transit traffic was NOT charged on the
spoke. It now says it is. A cost model predating that change under-counts.
A PEERING IS TWO RESOURCES, NOT ONE
Initiated
one link only — create the second
Connected
both links exist — only now is it established
Disconnected
one link was deleted — delete the SURVIVOR and recreate BOTH
You cannot repair half a peering by adding the missing half back.
FOUR SETTINGS PER SIDE — ONLY ONE IS ON BY DEFAULT
ON Allow access to this VNet
— also makes the VirtualNetwork tag include the peer
off Allow forwarded traffic
— a permission, not a path: UDRs are separate
off Allow gateway transit
— the peer must actually contain a gateway
off Use remote gateway
— one peering only, and not if you have your own
Ticking the first box is what widens AllowVNetInBound to include the peer.
WHAT GLOBAL PEERING CHANGES — LESS THAN EXPECTED, THEN MORE
Not bandwidth: no restriction, local or global. The VM size is the only limit.
But resources behind a BASIC load balancer are unreachable via its front-end IP over global peering.
Affected: VMs and scale sets behind basic LBs, Azure Managed Redis, Application Gateway v1, Service
Fabric, API Management stv1, Entra Domain Services, Logic Apps, HDInsight, Batch, ASE v1 and v2.
Escape hatch: reach them directly on their private IPs. Standard load balancers work over both.
All public, China and government regions — but never across clouds.
THE OPERATIONAL FACTS
· Names do NOT resolve across a peering with default Azure DNS. Private DNS is a dependency,
not an extra — IP works, hostnames fail, and the peering looks healthy throughout.
· A peered VNet cannot be moved: delete the peering, move it, recreate the peering.
· Removing the remote half needs read and delete rights on the REMOTE virtual network.
· For a temporary cut, deselect allow-access rather than deleting a link.
· Peering beats a gateway connecting the same pair — the gateway becomes idle cost.
· Point-to-site clients must re-download to pick up the new routes.
Same-region peered resources see the same latency as within one VNet, and MACsec covers traffic between datacentres.
Past a hand-manageable mesh: Virtual Network Manager does 1,000 spokes to a hub, or a 3,000-VNet mesh, as one object.
